title: Prevent workloads from running privileged containers
description: Prevent application workloads from running privileged containers in EKS Auto Mode by enforcing Pod Security Standards through Pod Security Admission or an equivalent admission policy engine. Restrict privileged workloads to only approved system or platform namespaces with a documented operational requirement. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.2.1 Prevent workloads from running privileged containers

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$ns:=.metadata.namespace}}{{$p:=.metadata.name}}{{range .spec.containers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.privileged}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{range .spec.initContainers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.privileged}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{range .spec.ephemeralContainers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.privileged}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($4=="true")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Configure Pod Security Admission on workload namespaces so privileged containers are denied when new pods are created. For this control, baseline is sufficient to block privileged containers, but restricted is the stronger setting for workload namespaces when the applications can meet the additional pod hardening requirements. EKS pod security documentation shows these controls being applied through namespace labels and explains that multiple modes can be used together for enforcement, warning, and audit visibility. Label each workload namespace to enforce restricted, or use baseline where restricted would break valid workloads. Add warn and audit labels during rollout so violations are visible to users and audit logs while enforcement blocks new noncompliant pods. Set the variable $NAMESPACE to the namespace name being updated.

title: Ensure access to Secrets is minimized and granted only where required
description: Verify that access to Kubernetes Secret objects in EKS Auto Mode is granted only to IAM principals, Kubernetes users or groups, and workload identities with a defined operational or application need. The review should cover EKS access entries and associated access policies, Kubernetes RBAC roles and bindings, and workload access paths tied to Kubernetes service accounts and EKS Pod Identity. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.2 Ensure access to Secrets is minimized and granted only where required

audit.command: Review every path that can grant access to Kubernetes Secrets in an EKS Auto Mode cluster. Start with EKS access entries and associated access policies, because Auto Mode uses the EKS API access-entry model. Then review Kubernetes RBAC, service accounts, Pod Identity associations for workloads that access AWS secret stores, and legacy aws-auth mappings only if the cluster uses API_AND_CONFIG_MAP. Effective access can come from overlapping EKS access policies, Kubernetes groups, and RBAC bindings, and access policy scope can be either cluster or namespace.

remediation.command: Start with EKS access entries and associated access policies, because EKS policies can grant Secrets access without native RBAC objects, and policies such as AmazonEKSAdminViewPolicy, AmazonEKSSecretReaderPolicy, and broader administrative policies can expose Secrets depending on scope. Then reduce unnecessary access in Kubernetes RBAC, service accounts, and any remaining legacy aws-auth mappings, and replace broad permissions with the narrowest namespace or workload scope that still supports the required function. • Remove or narrow EKS access policy associations that expose Secrets, and prefer namespace access within the cluster wherever possible. If AWS managed access policies are still broader than required, use access entries with Kubernetes group assignments and custom Kubernetes RBAC to grant the exact permissions needed.

title: Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used
description: Default service accounts in EKS Auto Mode should not be used as the active identity for ordinary application or automation workloads. If a Pod does not specify a service account, Kubernetes automatically assigns the namespace default service account, and that account can authenticate to the Kubernetes API through its mounted token. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Fails when a default service account does not set automountServiceAccountToken: false or is bound to a Role/ClusterRole.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.5 Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used

audit.command:
sa=$(kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{if eq .metadata.name "default"}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.automountServiceAccountToken}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
rb=$(kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$b:=.metadata.name}}{{$bn:=.metadata.namespace}}{{range .subjects}}{{if eq .kind "ServiceAccount"}}{{if eq .name "default"}}{{if .namespace}}{{.namespace}}{{else}}{{$bn}}{{end}} {{$b}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$sa" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && $2!="false" {print "automount: " $1}')
bad2=$(printf '%s
' "$rb" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex {print "binding: " $0}')
if [ -z "$bad$bad2" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
%s
' "$bad" "$bad2" | grep . | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Create dedicated service accounts for workloads that need Kubernetes API access, or EKS Pod Identity, and update those workloads to explicitly set serviceAccountName rather than relying on the namespace default service account. For workloads that do not need Kubernetes API access, disable service account token auto mounting and avoid using the default service account as the active workload identity. Also review the default service account in each namespace and ensure it is not bound to unnecessary RBAC permissions. Modify the default service account in each application namespace to set: automountServiceAccountToken: false Then validate workload manifests, because a Pod automountServiceAccountToken setting can override the service account setting, and workloads that actually need Kubernetes API access must use an explicitly assigned service account instead of inheriting default.

title: Ensure that Service Account Tokens are only mounted where necessary
description: Service account tokens in EKS Auto Mode should be mounted only for Pods that require Kubernetes API access or an explicitly configured workload identity flow. EKS supports disabling automatic token mounting at the Pod or ServiceAccount level, and workloads that need AWS access through EKS Pod Identity, or any remaining IRSA configuration, should use a dedicated service account rather than relying on broad default token mounting. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Reports pods with an auto-mounted service account token (kube-api-access-* volume).
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.6 Ensure that Service Account Tokens are only mounted where necessary

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.metadata.name}}{{range .spec.volumes}} {{.name}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($0 ~ / kube-api-access-/)')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Apply the following steps to reduce unnecessary service account token mounting in EKS Auto Mode: • Set automountServiceAccountToken to false for Pods and ServiceAccounts that do not require Kubernetes API access. This reduces unnecessary default token auto mounting. • Update workloads to use a dedicated serviceAccountName only where a service account token is operationally required, instead of inheriting token behavior from the namespace default service account. Each application should use its own dedicated service account. • For workloads that need AWS access, use EKS Pod Identity, or any remaining IRSA configuration already approved for the cluster, with a dedicated service account rather than broad default token mounting. Both models associate AWS permissions to a Kubernetes service account for a specific workload boundary.

title: Standardize EKS cluster access by using access entries, policies, and permissions
description: EKS Auto Mode provides the Cluster Access Management API, access entries, and associated access policies as the recommended way to manage IAM principal access to the Kubernetes API. This model is preferred over the deprecated aws-auth ConfigMap for cluster access management, supports cluster or namespace permissions, and can also reference Kubernetes groups when native Role, ClusterRole, RoleBinding, or ClusterRoleBinding objects are needed for ... Requires the aws CLI with eks:DescribeCluster; the cluster comes from EKS_CLUSTER and the region from AWS_REGION/AWS_PROFILE. Checks the authentication mode is API or API_AND_CONFIG_MAP; review access entry scopes separately.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.7 Standardize EKS cluster access by using access entries, policies, and permissions

audit.command:
m=$(aws eks describe-cluster --name "${EKS_CLUSTER:?set EKS_CLUSTER}" --query cluster.accessConfig.authenticationMode --output text) || exit 1
case "$m" in API|API_AND_CONFIG_MAP) echo compliant;; *) echo "noncompliant: authenticationMode=$m";; esac

remediation.command: Log in to the AWS Management Console, navigate Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service > Clusters and click on your EKS cluster. Go to the Access tab and click on Manage in the Access Configuration section. Under Cluster Authentication Mode for Cluster Access settings choose one of the following. • EKS API Use this as the target mode for EKS Auto Mode clusters after access has been migrated to access entries and associated access policies. The cluster will source authenticated IAM principals only from EKS access entry APIs • EKS API and ConfigMap Use this only when legacy aws-auth ConfigMap access must still coexist during migration or for an approved compatibility need.

title: Limit use of the Bind, Impersonate and Escalate permissions in the Kubernetes cluster
description: In EKS Auto Mode, bind, impersonate, and escalate should be limited to identities with a documented administrative need, because these permissions belong to native Kubernetes RBAC and affect who can obtain or act with Kubernetes permissions. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.8 Limit use of the Bind, Impersonate and Escalate permissions in the Kubernetes cluster

audit.command: Review EKS Auto Mode custom Kubernetes RBAC to identify any users, groups, or service accounts granted bind, escalate, or impersonate through custom Kubernetes Role or ClusterRole objects. Determine which subjects receive those permissions through RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding assignments, and validate that each assignment is required for a defined administrative function.

remediation.command: Remove bind, escalate, and impersonate permissions from any custom Role or ClusterRole that does not require them for an approved administrative function. In EKS, use access entries and associated access policies for standard cluster access wherever possible, and reserve custom Kubernetes RBAC for cases where the predefined access policies do not meet the requirement. Where these permissions are still necessary, keep them as narrowly as possible and avoid assigning them to workload service accounts or broadly shared Kubernetes groups. • Update each affected custom Role to remove unnecessary bind, escalate, or impersonate permissions. • Update each affected custom ClusterRole so it retains only the specific elevated permission that is explicitly required. • Replace broad assignments with lower privilege roles, and reduce scope from cluster to namespace where possible.

title: Restrict webhook configuration access to approved identities
description: Access to ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration objects in EKS Auto Mode should be limited to tightly controlled cluster administrative identities. These objects define admission webhooks that intercept Kubernetes API requests before they are accepted, and they apply at cluster scope rather than namespace scope. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.11 Restrict webhook configuration access to approved identities

audit.command: Audit this control by identifying who can manage cluster ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration resources, and confirm that webhook definitions are limited to approved admission use cases in EKS Auto Mode. Review whether cluster access is managed through access entries and associated access policies or through Kubernetes groups and native RBAC, because EKS access entries are the primary cluster access model and Kubernetes group authorization still depends on manually managed Role, ClusterRole, RoleBinding, and ClusterRoleBinding objects.

remediation.command: Remove permission to create, update, patch, or delete ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration objects from broad ClusterRole and Role assignments, and rebind that access only to tightly controlled cluster identities. In EKS, use access entries and associated access policies for standard cluster access wherever possible, and reserve native Kubernetes RBAC for cases where the predefined access policies do not meet the requirement. Keep webhook configuration management limited to a small set of approved administrative identities, because these objects sit directly in the admission path and operate at cluster scope. For EKS Auto Mode, treat this as a cluster administrative permission and do not leave it reachable through broad Kubernetes group mappings or legacy ConfigMap access paths.

title: Minimize access to the service account token creation
description: Access to service account token creation in EKS Auto Mode should be limited to tightly controlled administrative or platform identities. Service accounts are a core Kubernetes identity type in EKS, projected service account tokens are used by workloads to authenticate, and Pods that do not need Kubernetes API access can avoid unnecessary token exposure by disabling automatic token mounting. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.12 Minimize access to the service account token creation

audit.command: Begin by confirming that service account token creation in EKS Auto Mode is limited to identities with an approved administrative or workload identity need. Review token issuance through native Kubernetes RBAC, not through access entries, because access entries govern IAM principal access to the Kubernetes API while service account tokens remain Kubernetes credentials used by workloads and service accounts.

remediation.command: Review all Role and ClusterRole definitions for access to the serviceaccounts/token subresource, and remove that permission from any user, group, CI/CD identity, or workload service account that does not have a documented operational requirement. In EKS, service account token issuance remains a Kubernetes RBAC concern, while IAM principal access to the Kubernetes API is managed separately through access entries and associated access policies. Token creation rights should remain limited to tightly controlled administrative or platform identities, because projected service account tokens are usable Kubernetes credentials and can also participate in workload identity flows such as EKS Pod Identity, or any remaining IRSA configuration already in use.

title: Prevent pods from sharing the host process ID namespace
description: Prevent pods from sharing the host process ID namespace by restricting spec.hostPID: true in EKS Auto Mode workload namespaces. In the EKS Pod Security Standards model, this is enforced through Pod Security Admission or an equivalent policy engine, and baseline or restricted enforcement should be used for workload namespaces where host process namespace sharing is not approved. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.2.2 Prevent pods from sharing the host process ID namespace

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.metadata.name}} {{.spec.hostPID}}{{"
"}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($3=="true")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Configure Pod Security Admission on workload namespaces so pods that request spec.hostPID: true are denied at admission time. Use enforce for remediation because it rejects violating pods. Use warn and audit as rollout and visibility controls, but do not treat them as enforcement. For this control, baseline is sufficient because it prohibits hostPID, while restricted provides stronger hardening for workload namespaces that can meet the additional requirements. Update each workload namespace with the restricted enforcement label. kubectl label ns $NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --overwrite If restricted is too disruptive for a valid workload namespace, enforce baseline as the minimum profile for this specific control.

title: Require workload pods to run with hostNetwork set to false
description: Require workload pods to run with hostNetwork set to false or leave it unset by restricting spec.hostNetwork: true in EKS Auto Mode workload namespaces. In EKS, Pod Security Standards can be applied through the built-in Pod Security Admission controller or an equivalent policy engine, using at least the baseline profile where host network sharing is not approved and restricted for stronger workload namespace hardening. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.2.4 Require workload pods to run with hostNetwork set to false

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.metadata.name}} {{.spec.hostNetwork}}{{"
"}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($3=="true")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Configure Pod Security Admission on workload namespaces so pods that request spec.hostNetwork: true are denied at admission time. For this control, baseline is sufficient because it prohibits hostNetwork, while restricted provides stronger hardening for workload namespaces that can meet the additional requirements. Use enforce' for remediation because it rejects violating pods and use warnandaudit` for visibility but do not treat it as enforcement. Configure each workload namespace to enforce the restricted profile. kubectl label ns $NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --overwrite If restricted is too disruptive for a valid workload namespace, enforce baseline as the minimum profile for this specific control.

title: Require workload containers to set allowPrivilegeEscalation to false
description: Require workload containers to set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: false in EKS Auto Mode workload namespaces so container processes cannot gain more privileges than their parent process. In EKS, Pod Security Standards can be applied through Pod Security Admission or a policy engine, and the restricted profile is the relevant profile for this control because it requires containers to set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Containers that do not explicitly set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false are reported.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.2.5 Require workload containers to set allowPrivilegeEscalation to false

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$ns:=.metadata.namespace}}{{$p:=.metadata.name}}{{range .spec.containers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.allowPrivilegeEscalation}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{range .spec.initContainers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.allowPrivilegeEscalation}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{range .spec.ephemeralContainers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.allowPrivilegeEscalation}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($4!="false")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Configure Pod Security Admission on workload namespaces so containers that do not explicitly set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false are denied at admission time. In EKS, use restricted for workload namespaces, or an equivalent policy engine, because restricted requires allowPrivilegeEscalation=false. Use enforce for actual remediation, since warn and audit only report violations and do not block pod creation. Configure each workload namespace to enforce the restricted profile. kubectl label ns $NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --overwrite Add warn and audit during rollout if you want visibility into violations before or alongside enforcement.

title: Mount secrets as files instead of environment variables
description: Secrets for EKS workloads are better exposed as mounted files than as environment variables. Kubernetes Secrets can be consumed either way, and AWS supports file delivery from AWS Secrets Manager and Parameter Store through the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.4.1 Mount secrets as files instead of environment variables

audit.command: Review workload manifests and identify any Pod, Deployment, DaemonSet, StatefulSet, Job, or CronJob that exposes secrets through environment variables instead of mounted files. Check for both direct secret references through env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef and bulk secret imports through envFrom[].secretRef, because either pattern exposes secret data as environment variables. Prefer workloads that consume secrets through mounted Secret volumes or file delivery from AWS secrets integrations instead.

remediation.command: Update workloads to consume secrets as mounted files instead of environment variables. Replace env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef and envFrom[].secretRef usage with Kubernetes Secret volumes or the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, and then update the application to read the secret from the mounted file path. This reduces the chance of secret values appearing in logs and aligns with the recommended file delivery pattern for EKS workloads. For Kubernetes Secrets, mount the Secret as a volume and update the application configuration to read from the mounted path rather than from environment variables.

title: Use external secret storage for sensitive values
description: Use external secret storage to manage sensitive application values in AWS Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store instead of relying only on native Kubernetes Secret objects. This approach lets EKS workloads consume secrets through integrations such as the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, while keeping secret lifecycle functions outside the cluster. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.4.2 Use external secret storage for sensitive values

audit.command: Audit the EKS Auto Mode cluster’s secrets architecture and verify that required workloads use an external secrets store such as AWS Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store instead of relying only on Kubernetes Secret objects. The audit should confirm both the integration path and the workload access model, because external secret storage in EKS commonly uses the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, plus pod IAM through EKS Pod Identity or IRSA.

remediation.command: Use AWS Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store as the primary store for application secrets. Update EKS workloads to retrieve those values through the AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider with the Secrets Store CSI Driver, using IAM through EKS Pod Identity or IRSA. This shifts encryption, access control, rotation, and auditing to AWS rather than leaving those functions primarily in cluster Secret objects. • Create the required secrets in AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, and define least privilege IAM permissions so each workload identity can read only the specific secrets it requires. • Install and configure the Secrets Store CSI Driver and AWS Secrets and Configuration Provider if they are not already present.

title: Enforce least privilege for ECR repositories storing EKS Auto Mode workload images
description: Least privilege access for Amazon ECR repositories helps limit who can pull, push, delete, or administer container images used by EKS Auto Mode workloads. This reduces unnecessary exposure of the image registry and helps ensure that only the identities required to support image pulls, image publishing, release promotion, and repository administration can access the repositories. EKS Auto Mode shifts more infrastructure management to AWS. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.1.2 Enforce least privilege for ECR repositories storing EKS Auto Mode workload images

audit.command: Review the IAM permissions and ECR repository policies that apply to repositories used by EKS Auto Mode workload images, and verify that access is limited to approved EKS Auto Mode Node IAM roles, CI/CD identities, cross-account principals, and repository administration roles. Confirm that runtime pull access is limited to the minimum ECR actions required for image retrieval, that push or administrative access is limited to the repositories and actions required, and that no unnecessary wildcard or broad cross-account access is present.

remediation.command: Enforce least privilege access for ECR repositories used by EKS Auto Mode workload images by separating image pull, image push, account access, and repository administration into different IAM roles and policy scopes. Grant the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role only the ECR permissions needed to authenticate and pull images, such as ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability, ecr:BatchGetImage, and ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer. Scope CI/CD and administrator access to the specific repositories and actions they require, and review both IAM identity based policies and ECR repository policies because ECR authorization can be affected by both. Separate ECR access by role. Use different roles for EKS Auto Mode runtime image pulls, CI/CD image pushes, account repository access, and repository administration. • Replace broad pull access with pull-only permissions where possible.

title: Restrict EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role to ECR pull-only permissions
description: Restricting ECR access for the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role to pull only permissions helps ensure that nodes can retrieve required container images without receiving broader registry visibility, image publishing, deletion, or administrative access. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.1.3 Restrict EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role to ECR pull-only permissions

audit.command: Review the IAM permissions and any ECR repository policies that apply to the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role, and verify that the role is limited to pull-only ECR access. For this control, focus on the Node IAM role assigned to EKS Auto Mode nodes. If the cluster also uses Fargate, review the Fargate pod execution role under a separate Fargate specific check. The EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role has key permissions that include pulling images from ECR, and the suggested node role policies include AmazonEKSWorkerNodeMinimalPolicy and AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly.

remediation.command: Enforce pull-only ECR access for the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role by limiting the role to the permissions required to authenticate to ECR and retrieve container image layers. The EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role should use AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly or equivalent permissions, together with the required EKS node permissions. Identify the EKS Auto Mode Node IAM role in scope. Use the role configured in the cluster’s Auto Mode compute configuration or the expected role name, such as AmazonEKSAutoNodeRole. Remove broader ECR managed policies from the Node IAM role. Detach AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly, AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPowerUser, AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryFullAccess, or similar broad policies from the role when it only needs image-pull access. ECR managed policies are general purpose, and customer-managed policies can further reduce permissions for specific use cases.

title: Use dedicated service accounts for EKS Auto Mode workload identities
description: Using dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for EKS Auto Mode workload identities helps isolate AWS permissions by application, job, or trust boundary instead of sharing a single identity across multiple workloads. This supports more controlled access to AWS services and reduces the blast radius if one workload is compromised or misconfigured. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Reports pods running as the namespace default service account.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.2.1 Use dedicated service accounts for EKS Auto Mode workload identities

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.metadata.name}} {{.spec.serviceAccountName}}{{"
"}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($3=="default" || $3=="<no")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Use dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for EKS Auto Mode workloads and map AWS access to those accounts through EKS Pod Identity, or IRSA where required. Create one least privilege IAM role per application or permission boundary, update workloads to reference the intended serviceAccountName, disable token automounting where Kubernetes API access is not needed, and restrict node instance profile access so pods cannot inherit broader node credentials. • Create a dedicated Kubernetes service account for each application or distinct AWS permission boundary instead of sharing the namespace default service account. • Associate that service account with a least privilege IAM role by using EKS Pod Identity where supported, or IRSA where Pod Identity is not supported or not selected. For EKS Pod Identity, create an association between the Kubernetes namespace, service account, and IAM role.

title: Encrypt EKS API data with customer managed KMS keys
description: Using customer managed KMS keys for EKS envelope encryption adds a customer controlled protection layer for Kubernetes API data stored through the EKS control plane, not only Kubernetes Secrets. This strengthens data at rest protection while allowing organizations to manage key ownership, rotation, policy, and audit visibility for the key used to protect EKS API data. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.3.1 Encrypt EKS API data with customer managed KMS keys

audit.command: Review the EKS cluster configuration and verify that EKS API data is protected with a customer managed KMS key, not only the default AWS owned envelope encryption key. For this control, the important check is whether the cluster is associated with a customer managed key for EKS envelope encryption. EKS Auto Mode supports envelope encryption for Kubernetes API data using AWS KMS, with options for AWS owned keys or customer managed keys. Review the cluster encryption configuration and confirm a customer managed KMS key ARN is associated with the cluster.

remediation.command: Configure the EKS Auto Mode cluster to use a customer managed KMS key for EKS envelope encryption so Kubernetes API data is protected with a customer controlled key encryption key. The key must already exist, be symmetric, support encrypt and decrypt operations, be in the same Region as the cluster, and have permissions that allow EKS to use it. The associate-encryption-config operation does not create a KMS key and does not encrypt arbitrary data directly. It associates an existing customer managed KMS key to the cluster for envelope encryption. In the EKS API, the association is still expressed with resources:["secrets"], but for current EKS envelope encryption, a customer managed key associated for Secrets is used as the key encryption key for Kubernetes API data protected by envelope encryption.

title: Enable private EKS API access and restrict public access to approved CIDRs
description: This recommendation reduces exposure of the EKS Kubernetes API server endpoint without requiring a private only design. The intended end state is that private endpoint access is enabled, and if the public endpoint remains enabled, public access is restricted to approved CIDR ranges instead of being open to all internet addresses. This preserves approved administration paths while reducing unnecessary internet exposure. Requires the aws CLI with eks:DescribeCluster; the cluster comes from EKS_CLUSTER and the region from AWS_REGION/AWS_PROFILE. Private access must be on and any public endpoint must not allow 0.0.0.0/0.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.4.1 Enable private EKS API access and restrict public access to approved CIDRs

audit.command:
out=$(aws eks describe-cluster --name "${EKS_CLUSTER:?set EKS_CLUSTER}" --query 'cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.[endpointPrivateAccess,endpointPublicAccess,join(`
`,publicAccessCidrs || `[]`)]' --output text) || exit 1
set -- $out
priv=$1; pub=$2; cidrs=${3:-}
if [ "$priv" != True ]; then echo "noncompliant: endpointPrivateAccess=$priv"
elif [ "$pub" = True ] && { [ -z "$cidrs" ] || printf '%s' "$cidrs" | grep -q '0\.0\.0\.0/0'; }; then echo "noncompliant: public endpoint open to $cidrs"
else echo compliant; fi

remediation.command: • Replace 203.0.113.5/32 with the approved administrator, VPN, automation, or egress CIDR range. • Add only the CIDR ranges required for approved access paths. • After the update completes, rerun the audit command. • Confirm private access is enabled. • Confirm public access is enabled only as intended. • Confirm the public CIDR list does not include unrestricted ranges such as 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0. • Remember that EKS API endpoint access remains a cluster endpoint configuration setting, even when EKS Auto Mode automates other cluster networking functions.

title: Enable private only EKS API access and disable public endpoint access
description: This recommendation is the strict private only version of API endpoint hardening. The intended end state is that the EKS Kubernetes API server endpoint is reachable only from inside the cluster VPC or from a connected private network, and there is no internet reachable public API endpoint. This is a Kubernetes API exposure decision, not an EKS Auto Mode workload networking setting. Requires the aws CLI with eks:DescribeCluster; the cluster comes from EKS_CLUSTER and the region from AWS_REGION/AWS_PROFILE.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.4.2 Enable private only EKS API access and disable public endpoint access

audit.command:
out=$(aws eks describe-cluster --name "${EKS_CLUSTER:?set EKS_CLUSTER}" --query 'cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.[endpointPrivateAccess,endpointPublicAccess]' --output text) || exit 1
set -- $out
if [ "$1" = True ] && [ "$2" = False ]; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: private=$1 public=$2"; fi

remediation.command: Enable private endpoint access and disable public endpoint access for the EKS Kubernetes API server. This removes direct internet reachability to the public API endpoint and requires cluster administration through the cluster VPC or a connected private network such as VPN, Transit Gateway, Direct Connect, or an approved management host inside the VPC. EKS allows public and private endpoint access to be configured separately, and the default for new clusters is public access enabled with private access disabled. Before applying this change, confirm that administrators, CI/CD runners, and operational tooling can reach the Kubernetes API through the private access path.

title: Deploy EKS Auto Mode nodes only in private subnets
description: This recommendation is about the EKS Auto Mode data plane, not the control plane. It means EKS Auto Mode nodes are placed only in private subnets and are not intended to have direct public internet exposure. In the common pattern, nodes run in private subnets while internet facing ingress resources are placed in public subnets. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.4.3 Deploy EKS Auto Mode nodes only in private subnets

audit.command: Review the EKS Auto Mode NodePool and NodeClass configuration to confirm nodes are placed only in private subnets. Validate the NodeClass subnet selection, subnet public IP behavior, and route table design. A compliant design uses subnets that do not auto assign public IPv4 addresses and do not route directly to an Internet Gateway. Review the NodePool and NodeClass configuration and confirm each NodePool references a NodeClass whose subnetSelectorTerms select only private subnets. The NodeClass should use private subnet IDs directly or private subnet tags.

remediation.command: For EKS Auto Mode nodes placed in public subnets, remediate by updating the NodeClass and NodePool design so Auto Mode provisions nodes only in private subnets. In EKS Auto Mode, subnet placement is controlled through NodeClass subnetSelectorTerms, and NodePools reference the NodeClass that defines the infrastructure configuration. If existing nodes were created from a NodeClass that selects public subnets, create or update a NodeClass that selects only private subnets, then move workloads to NodePools that reference the corrected NodeClass. • Create or update the NodeClass so subnetSelectorTerms selects only private subnet IDs or private subnet tags • Confirm the selected subnets do not auto assign public IPv4 addresses and their route tables do not send 0.0.0.0/0 directly to an Internet Gateway.

title: Use TLS certificates for EKS Auto Mode load balancer listeners
description: Using TLS certificates on EKS Auto Mode load balancer listeners protects client traffic by presenting a trusted server certificate and negotiating encrypted HTTPS or TLS connections at the listener. In EKS Auto Mode, this commonly means configuring TLS on a Network Load Balancer created from a Kubernetes Service or specifying certificate ARNs for an Application Load Balancer created from IngressClassParams and Ingress resources so externally ... The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.4.4 Use TLS certificates for EKS Auto Mode load balancer listeners

audit.command: Review all client facing EKS Auto Mode load balancers and verify that listeners use HTTPS or TLS with a valid certificate. For NLB backed Service resources, listener TLS is configured with annotations such as aws-load-balancer-ssl-cert for the ACM certificate ARN and aws-load-balancer-ssl-ports for the encrypted listener ports. For ALB backed Ingress resources, the certificate is configured through IngressClassParams using certificateARNs.

remediation.command: Configure every client facing EKS Auto Mode load balancer listener to use HTTPS or TLS with a valid certificate so client to load balancer traffic is encrypted in transit. For NLB backed Service resources, add the ACM certificate ARN and encrypted listener ports in the Service annotations. For ALB backed Ingress resources, configure HTTPS listener behavior through IngressClassParams and associate the required ACM certificate ARN using certificateARNs. If encryption is required beyond the load balancer, implement backend TLS separately because listener TLS alone protects only the client facing connection. • Add a valid ACM certificate to each client facing NLB or ALB listener that should serve encrypted traffic. • For NLB Services, set aws-load-balancer-ssl-cert to the ACM certificate ARN and aws-load-balancer-ssl-ports to the required listener ports.

title: Use EKS access entries for IAM principal Kubernetes access
description: Using EKS access entries centralizes how IAM principals are granted access to the Kubernetes API and lets cluster access be managed through Amazon EKS instead of relying on manual aws-auth ConfigMap updates. This gives a cleaner access management model for users and roles that need to work with Kubernetes resources in the cluster. Requires the aws CLI with eks:DescribeCluster; the cluster comes from EKS_CLUSTER and the region from AWS_REGION/AWS_PROFILE. Checks the authentication mode is API or API_AND_CONFIG_MAP.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.5.1 Use EKS access entries for IAM principal Kubernetes access

audit.command:
m=$(aws eks describe-cluster --name "${EKS_CLUSTER:?set EKS_CLUSTER}" --query cluster.accessConfig.authenticationMode --output text) || exit 1
case "$m" in API|API_AND_CONFIG_MAP) echo compliant;; *) echo "noncompliant: authenticationMode=$m";; esac

remediation.command: Configure the cluster to use EKS access entries for IAM principal access management, then create and scope access entries for each required IAM role or user. For EKS Auto Mode, access entries should be the primary access model because Auto Mode uses access entries and they cannot be disabled. This remediation typically starts by enabling the access entry API through the cluster authentication mode, then moving existing access management from legacy aws-auth ConfigMap mappings to access entries with EKS access policies, Kubernetes RBAC group mappings, or both. Moving from CONFIG_MAP to API_AND_CONFIG_MAP is the recommended transition path when legacy mappings still need to be preserved during migration. Update the cluster authentication mode to API_AND_CONFIG_MAP.

title: Grant AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy only where full cluster administration is required
description: Grant AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy only to IAM principals that require unrestricted, cluster administrative control. In EKS Auto Mode, cluster access is built on EKS access entries and the EKS API authentication mode, and the initial bootstrap administrator access for the cluster creator can be disabled, so full administrator rights should be assigned deliberately rather than used as the default operating model. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.1 Grant AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy only where full cluster administration is required

audit.command: For EKS Auto Mode, this setting should be audited through EKS access entries and associated access policies, because Auto Mode uses the EKS API access model and you cannot disable access entries on an Auto Mode cluster. AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy is the AWS managed policy that grants cluster administrator access, so the audit should confirm that it is present only on principals with a documented need for full cluster administration. Identify the IAM principal you want to review and confirm its principal ARN and target cluster name.

remediation.command: In EKS Auto Mode, this setting should be updated through EKS access entries and associated access policies rather than older cluster access methods. Auto Mode relies on the EKS access entry model to authorize IAM principals for Kubernetes access, and STANDARD access entries support adding or removing AWS-managed EKS access policies with either cluster or namespace permissions. Where those predefined policies do not provide the required level of restriction, administrators can use access entries with Kubernetes group assignments and apply custom Kubernetes RBAC for fine grained control. Identify principals that do not need full cluster administration. Review each IAM user or role that currently has AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy and confirm whether its duties truly require unrestricted access across all Kubernetes API groups, resources, verbs, and non-resource URLs.

title: Minimize wildcard use in Roles and ClusterRoles
description: Verify that Kubernetes Role and ClusterRole objects in EKS Auto Mode do not use wildcard entries such as * for verbs, resources, or apiGroups unless a documented administrative or platform requirement exists. The review should also include the RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding objects that assign those roles to users, groups, or service accounts, because EKS Auto Mode uses access entries for IAM principal access, but still supports native ... The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.3 Minimize wildcard use in Roles and ClusterRoles

audit.command: Begin by reviewing custom Kubernetes Role and ClusterRole objects in EKS Auto Mode to identify any use of wildcard entries such as * for verbs, resources, or apiGroups. In EKS, this review should cover native RBAC objects, access entries that reference Kubernetes groups, service accounts, and any remaining aws-auth mappings only where ConfigMap based access still applies, because EKS supports access through both access entries and Kubernetes RBAC, and it also creates its own platform RBAC objects that should be distinguished from customer defined permissions.

remediation.command: Begin by replacing wildcard permissions in custom Role and ClusterRole objects with explicitly enumerated verbs, resources, and apiGroups that match the approved operational need. In EKS, this remediation should focus on customer managed RBAC objects, the bindings that assign them, access entries that reference Kubernetes groups, and service accounts used by workloads or cluster components. EKS guidance favors specific access through access entries and using custom RBAC only when predefined access policies do not meet the requirement, especially for service accounts used by add-ons, DaemonSets, and CSI drivers. • Replace wildcard values in custom Role and ClusterRole rules with the specific verbs, resources, and apiGroups the function actually requires.

title: Minimize access to create pods
description: The ability to create Pods in EKS Auto Mode is a high risk permission that should be limited to approved deployment and operational functions. In EKS, Pod creation can be granted through associated access policies or native Kubernetes RBAC, and policies such as AmazonEKSAdminPolicy and AmazonEKSEditPolicy include create access on pods. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.4 Minimize access to create pods

audit.command: Begin by reviewing every path that can grant the ability to create Pods in EKS Auto Mode. Start with access entries and associated access policies, because Auto Mode uses the EKS API access-entry model, and AmazonEKSAdminPolicy and AmazonEKSEditPolicy include create access for pods. Then review Kubernetes RBAC, service accounts, and Pod security controls, because Pod creation can allow an identity to launch workloads under available service accounts and potentially exercise both Kubernetes and AWS permissions.

remediation.command: Begin with access entries and associated access policies, because AmazonEKSAdminPolicy and AmazonEKSEditPolicy include create access for pods, and access policies can be to the cluster or to specific namespaces. Then reduce unnecessary permissions in Kubernetes RBAC, service accounts, and Pod security controls so Pod creation is limited to approved deployment paths and the smallest practical workload boundary. • Remove or narrow access policy associations that allow Pod creation, and prefer namespace access over cluster scope wherever possible. If predefined access policies are still broader than required, use access entries with Kubernetes group assignments and custom RBAC to grant the exact permissions needed. • Replace broad RBAC permissions on pods, deployments, daemonsets, statefulsets, jobs, and cronjobs with the smallest Role or ClusterRole that supports the approved function.

title: Grant persistent storage provisioning access only where StorageClasses and PersistentVolumeClaims are required
description: Permission to create persistent storage in EKS Auto Mode should be granted only where it is required. In EKS, this includes direct creation of PersistentVolume objects and, more commonly in Auto Mode, the ability to trigger dynamic provisioning through PersistentVolumeClaim and StorageClass use, because EKS storage integrations such as the Amazon EBS CSI driver and EKS Auto Mode can automatically provision backing storage when applications ... The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.9 Grant persistent storage provisioning access only where StorageClasses and PersistentVolumeClaims are required

audit.command: Review EKS RBAC to identify any users, groups, or service accounts that can create PersistentVolume, PersistentVolumeClaim, or StorageClass resources. In EKS, this review should give particular attention to PersistentVolumeClaim and StorageClass permissions because persistent storage is commonly provisioned dynamically through StorageClass and PersistentVolumeClaim objects in EKS Auto Mode rather than by manually creating PersistentVolume objects.

remediation.command: Remove persistent storage creation rights from any user, group, or service account that does not require them, and replace broad assignments with the lowest privilege role and narrowest scope possible. In EKS, prioritize PersistentVolumeClaim and StorageClass permissions because persistent storage is commonly provisioned dynamically through the EKS Auto Mode block storage path rather than by manually creating PersistentVolume objects. Limit direct PersistentVolume and StorageClass administration to approved administrators, and allow workloads to use only the PersistentVolumeClaim access required for approved storage classes. After changes are made, verify that required applications can still provision storage through the intended EKS Auto Mode storage class and PVC path.

title: Grant nodes/proxy access only to approved identities that require node-level access
description: Access to the nodes/proxy subresource in EKS Auto Mode should be limited to identities with a documented node administration or troubleshooting need. This review should cover custom Role and ClusterRole rules, RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding assignments, and any service accounts that receive node subresource access. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.10 Grant nodes/proxy access only to approved identities that require node-level access

audit.command: Review EKS Auto Mode custom Kubernetes RBAC to identify custom Role and ClusterRole objects that grant access to the nodes/proxy subresource, and validate that each permission is required for an approved troubleshooting, maintenance, or platform administration function. Focus this review on customer RBAC because EKS creates its own default RBAC identities for cluster components, while customer defined node-proxy access is usually introduced through native Kubernetes RBAC.

remediation.command: Reduce custom RBAC access to the nodes/proxy API path so it is limited to approved administrative identities that require node access. In EKS, use access entries and associated access policies for standard cluster access wherever possible, and reserve custom Kubernetes RBAC for cases where the predefined access policies do not meet the requirement. Keep nodes/proxy limited to tightly controlled troubleshooting, maintenance, or platform administration use cases, and avoid assigning it to workload service accounts or broadly shared Kubernetes groups. • Remove nodes/proxy from any custom Role or ClusterRole where node proxy is not explicitly required. • Where some node access is still needed, replace nodes/proxy with narrower permissions on only the specific resources and verbs required, and reduce scope from ClusterRole to namespace Role where the function allows it.

title: Require workload pods to run with hostIPC set to false
description: Require workload pods to run with hostIPC set to false or leave it unset by restricting spec.hostIPC: true in EKS Auto Mode workload namespaces. In the EKS Pod Security Standards model, this is done through Pod Security Admission or an equivalent policy engine, and baseline or restricted enforcement should be applied to workload namespaces where host IPC namespace sharing is not approved. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.2.3 Require workload pods to run with hostIPC set to false

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.metadata.name}} {{.spec.hostIPC}}{{"
"}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($3=="true")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Configure Pod Security Admission on workload namespaces so pods that request spec.hostIPC: true are denied at admission time. For this control, baseline is sufficient because it prohibits hostIPC, while restricted provides stronger hardening for workload namespaces that can meet the additional requirements. Use enforce for remediation because it rejects violating pods. Use warn and audit for rollout visibility, but do not treat them as enforcement. Configure each workload namespace to enforce the restricted profile. kubectl label ns $NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --overwrite If restricted is too disruptive for a valid workload namespace, enforce baseline as the minimum profile for this specific control.

title: Enable Network Policy enforcement for EKS Auto Mode
description: EKS Auto Mode provides AWS managed VPC pod networking with built-in support for pod network policies. For this control, enable Network Policy enforcement by configuring the EKS Auto Mode Network Policy Controller, which is done by applying the amazon-vpc-cni ConfigMap with enable-network-policy-controller: true in the kube-system namespace. Requires kubectl read access to kube-system; checks the amazon-vpc-cni ConfigMap enables the Network Policy Controller.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.3.1 Enable Network Policy enforcement for EKS Auto Mode

audit.command:
v=$(kubectl get configmap amazon-vpc-cni -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.data.enable-network-policy-controller}') || exit 1
if [ "$v" = true ]; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: enable-network-policy-controller=${v:-not-set}"; fi

remediation.command: Enable Network Policy enforcement for EKS Auto Mode by applying or updating the amazon-vpc-cni ConfigMap in the kube-system namespace with enable-network-policy-controller: true. There is no separate EKS cluster update command for this setting in Auto Mode. Create a file named enable-network-policy.yaml: apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata: name: amazon-vpc-cni namespace: kube-system data: enable-network-policy-controller: "true" Apply the ConfigMap: kubectl apply -f enable-network-policy.yaml Validate the setting: kubectl get configmap amazon-vpc-cni -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.data.enable-network-policy-controller}{"\n"}' • After the controller is enabled, apply the required Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources or supported EKS network policy resources for the workloads that need traffic restrictions.

title: Restrict workload traffic with Kubernetes Network Policies
description: EKS Auto Mode supports Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources for namespace Layer 3 and Layer 4 pod traffic isolation, and also supports broader EKS network policy capabilities such as ClusterNetworkPolicy and ApplicationNetworkPolicy where applicable. Workload isolation depends on the relevant workloads actually being covered by NetworkPolicy, ClusterNetworkPolicy, or other supported EKS network policy resources. Reported as a manual review because it needs site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.3.2 Restrict workload traffic with Kubernetes Network Policies

audit.command: Review the Kubernetes network policy in the EKS Auto Mode cluster and verify that every required workload is selected by either namespace NetworkPolicy, ApplicationNetworkPolicy, or a cluster ClusterNetworkPolicy. A separate policy in every namespace is not always required because ClusterNetworkPolicy can apply shared controls across all workloads or selected namespaces, while namespace policies can provide application segmentation. EKS Auto Mode supports different network policy types, including standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, DNS-based policies, and cluster rules.

remediation.command: Create and apply Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, ApplicationNetworkPolicy, or ClusterNetworkPolicy objects so every required workload is explicitly covered by policy. Use namespace NetworkPolicy for workload Network and Transport layer segmentation, use ApplicationNetworkPolicy when DNS egress filtering is required, and use ClusterNetworkPolicy when a shared security posture must apply across multiple namespaces or workload groups. EKS Auto Mode supports these network policy patterns for pod traffic isolation and centralized network access controls. • Set default deny and then add only the ingress and egress rules needed for approved traffic such as DNS, required service-to-service flows, and authorized external destinations. Use specific selectors and destinations rather than broad namespace, pod, IP, or domain patterns whenever possible.

title: Use dedicated namespaces to separate workload boundaries
description: Namespaces create administrative boundaries in EKS by dividing a cluster into logical partitions for teams, applications, environments, or tenants. They are a core building block for soft multitenancy, and several controls used to separate workloads, including quotas, network policies, and service accounts, are defined to the namespace. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.5.1 Use dedicated namespaces to separate workload boundaries

audit.command: Verify that namespaces are being used as intentional administrative boundaries for groups, applications, or environments in the EKS Auto Mode cluster. Namespaces should be paired with scoped access controls and namespace governance such as quotas, limits, service accounts, and network policies. In EKS Auto Mode, customers remain responsible for application containers, workload access, and namespace governance even though AWS manages more of the underlying infrastructure.

remediation.command: Create dedicated namespaces for groups, applications, or environments that need separate administrative scope, and move workloads out of the default namespace. Strengthen each namespace boundary with targeted access, quotas, limits, service accounts, and network policies, and reduce cluster permissions that bypass the intended separation model. EKS Auto Mode manages more of the data plane infrastructure, but namespace design, workload placement, access control, and application governance remain customer responsibilities. Create dedicated namespaces for each group, application, or environment that needs its own administrative boundary. kubectl create namespace $NAMESPACE • Move user workloads out of the default namespace and into the appropriate managed namespace.

title: Enable ECR enhanced scanning for EKS Auto Mode workload images
description: Container image vulnerability scanning helps strengthen the security of EKS Auto Mode workload images by identifying known software weaknesses before or after images are deployed. Because EKS Auto Mode manages more of the cluster infrastructure while customers remain responsible for application containers and pods, image scanning remains a customer controlled workload security requirement. Requires the aws CLI (ecr:GetRegistryScanningConfiguration) in the cluster region; repository filter coverage still needs review.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.1.1 Enable ECR enhanced scanning for EKS Auto Mode workload images

audit.command:
t=$(aws ecr get-registry-scanning-configuration --query scanningConfiguration.scanType --output text) || exit 1
if [ "$t" = ENHANCED ]; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: scanType=$t"; fi

remediation.command: Enable ECR enhanced scanning for the private registry in each Region that stores images used by EKS Auto Mode workloads. Use registry scanning configuration rather than repository scan on push configuration, because the repository PutImageScanningConfiguration API is being deprecated in favor of registry configuration. Enhanced scanning integrates ECR with Amazon Inspector to provide automated and continuous scanning for operating system and programming language package vulnerabilities. Identify the ECR repositories and Regions that provide images to EKS Auto Mode workloads. Use the image references from Kubernetes workloads to determine which ECR repositories must be covered by enhanced scanning. Enable enhanced scanning for the private registry in each applicable Region. When no rules are specified, ECR sets enhanced scanning to continuous scanning for all repositories by default.

title: Restrict EKS Auto Mode workload images to approved registries
description: Restricting EKS Auto Mode workload images to approved registries helps reduce software supply chain risk by ensuring workloads are sourced only from trusted image locations. Approved registry controls provide a workload guardrail that complements image scanning, image signing, and deployment governance. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.1.4 Restrict EKS Auto Mode workload images to approved registries

audit.command: Review the image sources currently used by the cluster and the admission controls that govern new deployments, then verify that EKS Auto Mode workload images are limited to approved registries only. EKS Auto Mode nodes are Kubernetes conformant, so standard Kubernetes policy enforcement tools can be used to limit workload configuration, including allowed image registries. Compare running workload image registry hostnames to the approved registry allowlist. Any image sourced from an unapproved registry is a finding.

remediation.command: Restrict EKS Auto Mode workload images to approved container registries by enforcing image source controls at admission time, rather than relying only on CI/CD checks or written standards. Enforcement is typically implemented with a policy admission controller such as Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper, or another validating admission path so image references are checked before the workload is admitted. EKS Auto Mode supports standard Kubernetes policy enforcement tools, making admission time registry restrictions appropriate for Auto Mode workload governance. Include internal ECR repositories, explicitly approved third-party registries, and required ECR registries for EKS add-ons, platform components, security agents, and operational tooling in the approved registry allowlist.

title: Avoid deploying workloads in the default namespace
description: Avoid placing application workloads in the default namespace, and instead deploy them into dedicated namespaces that reflect the intended group, application, environment, or tenant boundary. In EKS, namespaces are the primary logical partition for organizing workloads and supporting soft multitenancy in a shared cluster. Requires kubectl read access; fails when the default namespace holds objects other than the kubernetes Service, kube-root-ca.crt ConfigMap and default ServiceAccount.
reference: CIS Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Auto Mode Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.5.2 Avoid deploying workloads in the default namespace

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods,services,configmaps,secrets,serviceaccounts,deployments,statefulsets,daemonsets,jobs,cronjobs,ingresses,roles,rolebindings -n default -o name) || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -v '^$' | sed 's#^\([a-z]*\)\.[^/]*/#\1/#' | grep -Evx 'service/kubernetes|configmap/kube-root-ca\.crt|serviceaccount/default')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s\n' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Move user workloads out of the default namespace and place them in dedicated namespaces that reflect the intended group, application, or environment boundary. In EKS, namespaces are the core logical partition for soft multi-tenancy, but they only become meaningful administrative boundaries when paired with access controls, service accounts, quotas, limits, and network policies. EKS Auto Mode manages infrastructure components such as compute, pod and service networking, load balancing, DNS, and storage, but workload placement and namespace governance remain customer responsibilities. • Create dedicated namespaces for each group, application, or environment that needs its own administrative boundary. • Redeploy or migrate user workloads from default into the appropriate dedicated namespace.
